lesson.title: Adding Arrows: Phasor Addition and Kirchhoff's Laws in the Frequency Domain
lesson.summary: Because a phasor is a fixed complex number, Kirchhoff's laws let same-frequency sinusoids be combined by ordinary vector addition instead of trigonometric identities.
lesson.body:
Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws hold at every instant in time, which means they also hold for phasors, since a phasor is simply a fixed complex number multiplying the same shared e^(jωt) factor in every term of the equation. Adding two sinusoidal voltages that share the same frequency is therefore equivalent to adding their phasors as complex numbers; the awkward step of adding two cosines with different phase angles using trigonometric sum-to-product identities is replaced by ordinary vector addition.

Complex numbers add most easily in rectangular form, so the standard method converts each phasor from polar form Vm∠θ to rectangular form Vm cos θ + jVm sin θ, adds the real parts together and the imaginary parts together separately, then converts the rectangular sum back to polar form if a magnitude and angle are wanted. Geometrically, on a phasor diagram, this is exactly tip-to-tail vector addition: draw the first phasor, then draw the second starting from the tip of the first, and the sum is the arrow from the origin to the final tip.

Return to the series RL circuit with R = 30 Ω and XL = 40 Ω carrying current I = 2.4∠−53.13° A. Kirchhoff's voltage law says the source voltage equals the resistor voltage plus the inductor voltage: V = VR + VL. The resistor voltage is in phase with current, VR = I × R = 2.4∠−53.13° × 30 = 72∠−53.13° V. The inductor voltage leads current by 90°, VL = I × XL∠90° = 2.4∠−53.13° × 40∠90° = 96∠36.87° V. Converting both to rectangular form: VR = 72(cos(−53.13°) + j sin(−53.13°)) = 72(0.6000 − j0.8000) = 43.2 − j57.6 V, and VL = 96(cos 36.87° + j sin 36.87°) = 96(0.8000 + j0.6000) = 76.8 + j57.6 V.

Adding real parts: 43.2 + 76.8 = 120.0. Adding imaginary parts: −57.6 + 57.6 = 0.0. The sum is 120.0 + j0.0 V, which converts back to polar form as 120∠0° V, exactly matching the source voltage that drove the circuit in the first place. The imaginary parts cancel precisely because the resistor and inductor voltages have complementary angles, −53.13° and 36.87° differ by exactly 90°, a direct algebraic reflection of the 3-4-5 right triangle formed by R, XL, and the impedance magnitude.

This same tip-to-tail addition applies just as well to Kirchhoff's current law at a node, where branch currents, rather than series voltages, are summed as phasors. The general lesson carries forward into every later phasor calculation: whenever two or more same-frequency sinusoidal quantities combine, either by physical superposition in a circuit or by simple bookkeeping, converting to phasors turns the problem into complex-number addition, exact, fast, and free of trigonometric identities.

Subtraction works the same way, term by term, and scaling a phasor by a real constant, as happens when multiplying a current phasor by a resistance, simply scales its magnitude while leaving its angle unchanged. Addition, subtraction, and real scaling are all that Kirchhoff's laws ever require in a linear AC circuit; the one new operation, multiplying two phasors together, as happens when combining current with impedance, both rotates and scales, and is treated separately in the complex impedance section that follows.
